newsitem.title: ALGERIA: Algeria kills GIA rebel commander wanted in France.
newsitem.headline: Algeria kills GIA rebel commander wanted in France.

text.p: Algerian security forces have killed an Islamist guerrilla commander suspected of masterminding the hijacking of an Air France airliner in 1994 and a wave of bombings in France, newspapers said on Monday.

The papers hailed the killing on Sunday of Rihane Yahia and three of his Armed Islamic Group (GIA) comrades in a raid on their hideout in Algiers as a "severe blow" to the guerrillas fighting to topple the government.

Yahia, alias Abdallah Krounfel, was wanted by the French police for his suspected role in a wave of bomb attacks in France in 1995 and was believed to be the mastermind of the 1994 Christmas hijacking in which three passengers were killed, El Watan newspaper said quoting an unnamed source.

Algerian security officials on Sunday reported the killing of Yahia and three others in a six-hour gunbattle in the Anassers district, southwest of Algiers, wihtout giving details on Yahia's background.
"The security forces have dealt a heavy blow to the terrorist groups. It has been a long time to see such a leading fundamentalist falling dead," said Le Matin newspaper.
Residents said the security forces blew up the roof of the apartment in the 11-storey block where Yahia and his aides took refuge.
Le Matin said the GIA assigned Yahia to supervise the bombings in Paris in 1995 before returning home as a military commander of the group in Algiers.
Wanted posters with Yahia's photo were posted across France, but he escaped the dragnet.

In one of GIA's most spectacular operations, gunmen hijacked an Air France plane in Algiers on Christmas Eve in 1994. Three passengers were killed before French commandos stormed the plane 54 hours later in Marseille and shot dead four hijackers.
The GIA responded by killing four foreign Roman Catholic priests in Algeria.

Yahia's death came days after the killing of Kaddour Abdenour, deputy chief of a smaller guerrilla faction, the Algerian Djihad Islamic Front (FIDA), in a similar raid in Algiers, security officials said.
La Tribune newspaper said the killings of the senior guerrilla commanders were the result of a "huge anti-terrorist operation carried out by the security forces in several regions of the country".
Algiers residents said security forces were out in large numbers in search operations in which more than 200 guerrillas have been killed in the past two months.
Algeria is gearing up for June 5 parliamentary elections and the authorities have promised to ensure security for the poll.
The North African country has been without parliament since 1992 when the authorities cancelled a general election in which radical Islamists had taken a huge lead.
About 60,000 people have died in the five years of violence pitting government forces against Moslem rebels.
